t: A Simple Way To Curb Side-Talking
q: Side-talking can be especially frustrating because, although it’s done out of earshot, it’s remarkably disruptive.
Furthermore, side-talking begets more side-talking, as students catch the contagion and pass it along to others.
What follows is a simple, four-step solution. And the best part is, because it’s a student-empowered strategy, you don’t even have to get involved.
Crossing the first two fingers and shaking lightly is a good way to go. It’s a gesture conspicuous enough for you to see from across the room and all students can perform it easily.
It’s important to emphasize that the gesture is nothing more than a polite reminder to a friend. It’s like saying, “I’m sorry, but I can’t talk right now.
But unlike struggling to figure out who is deserving of a consequence, and getting it wrong much of the time, you’ll be able to tell exactly who the culprit is.
x: Linsin offers a four-step, student-empowered strategy for reducing disruptive side-talking without requiring teacher involvement in every incident.
Step 1: Clearly define side-talking for students, including any contexts where limited talking is allowed.

Step 2: Provide students a simple, non-offensive hand gesture (e.g., crossed fingers, lightly shaken) to signal 'I can't talk right now.'
Step 4: Emphasize the gesture is a polite reminder, not an aggressive rebuke, and pair it with a quick nod as the appropriate response.

t: Why You Shouldn’t Use A Hand Signal For Quiet Attention iet-attention/
q: The problem, however, is that even at its best, a hand signal is insufficient for such an important aspect of classroom management.
In other words, unless you already have their attention, a hand signal will take time to domino around the class—especially in a noisy, collaborative learning environment.
The problem with hand signals is that they’re not as clear, as detailed, or as descriptive as a few, simple words can be.

And nothing works better than asking, “Can I have your attention please?” This routine-prompting question communicates precisely what you want, works no matter where you are, and reaches every student at the same time.
It's common for teachers to hold up their quiet signal while at the same time offering reminders, warnings, and admonitions. But this only adds to the confusion.
A single, succinct verbal cue, on the other hand, is a once for all command that stays in play until you say otherwise.
x: Combining a hand signal with verbal reminders and warnings adds confusion rather than clarity.
A hand signal for quiet requires waiting for it to visually 'domino' around the room, wasting time especially in noisy settings.

The recommended alternative is a single verbal cue—'Can I have your attention please?'—that reaches every student simultaneously.

t: How To Build Effortless Rapport With Students
q: Rapport provides the good vibrations between you and your class that makes your classroom management plan matter.
The simple truth is that the better rapport you have with your students, the easier classroom management becomes.
You see, rapport comes effortlessly to those who manage their classroom without causing friction with students.
Like clockwork, students will begin testing the behavioral waters early in the school year to see if you really do mean what you say.
And hereafter, with the once-bright rays of rapport all but faded, both parties begin the slow, guarded limp onward, day after day, wary of each other but just getting through it.
No, rapport is nothing more than a willingness to enjoy your students combined with a near-obsessive reliance on your classroom management plan.
x: Rapport gives a classroom management plan its 'teeth,' making students genuinely reluctant to disappoint the teacher.

t: Why Picking Your Battles Is A Poor Strategy
q: Picking your battles will prevent you from ever turning around difficult students or creating the well-behaved classroom you really want.
Choosing to respond to misbehavior sometimes and not others breeds resentment—because it’s unfair and students know it.
Whenever you fail to follow your classroom management plan as promised, your integrity takes a hit.
When teachers speak of picking their battles, they're referring to having a confrontation. In other words, they intend to lecture, scold, question, or otherwise persuade students into compliance.
With confrontation and inconsistency equal parts of the toxic brew, picking your battles is like shooting yourself in the foot and pulling the rug out from under yourself at the same time.
For there is no need, not with a well-taught classroom management plan to do the heavy lifting for you.
x: Linsin pushes back against the popular advice to 'pick your battles' with difficult students, arguing it prevents teachers from ever turning around challenging behavior.

He lists a series of harms caused by selective enforcement: it breeds resentment and perceived favoritism, erodes trust, invites confrontation and arguing, and unnerves students who can't predict when a rule will…
The alternative is a consistently followed classroom management plan that removes the need to selectively engage at all.

t: The Best Incentive You Could Ever Give
q: Because I believe it’s a mistake to reward students for good behavior, I’m often asked, “So, then, the stickers, prizes, and such . . . should teachers refrain from giving them out at all?
Anything that whiffs of bribery should be avoided. No doubt about it.

Instead of doling out prizes based on what you receive in return (i.e. good behavior), you'll hand them out for no reason at all. In other words, they become no longer an incentive in the traditional sense, but a free gift.
A common complaint from teachers is that they’re under-appreciated by students. But this is a natural consequence of using rewards in exchange for good behavior.
The dance party isn’t a reward, however, and it isn’t a strategy. It’s nothing more than an expression of joy, an uninhibited celebration of another week of learning together.
There is no heartless exchange of goods and services. There is no bribery or manipulation. There is no “do this and get that“ culture to produce envy and jealousy.
